About the question text

Each NCERT question is shown in full above its solution, with its textbook location. The solutions are our own. This chapter has no intext questions. The three exercises have 12 numbered questions and 41 parts, and every part is solved separately below. Where a question asks for a graph, the solution gives the tables of values and describes the finished graph exactly, so you can draw it yourself and compare.

How every solution is laid out: Given / Asked → Concept used (and why it applies here) → Steps, one per line, with the reason in words → Check → ✅ Final answer → Common trap.

Exercise 3.1

Exercise 3.1, Q1 (i)Girls and boys in a quiz3 marks

Form the pair of linear equations in the following problems, and find their solutions graphically.
(i) 10 students of Class X took part in a Mathematics quiz. If the number of girls is 4 more than the number of boys, find the number of boys and girls who took part in the quiz.
Print graph paper

Given: 10 students in all; girls are 4 more than boys. Asked: a pair of equations, and its solution from a graph.

Concept used: the graphical method (Topic 2) after forming the equations (Topic 6). Why it applies: the question asks for the solution "graphically".

  1. 1

    Let the number of girls be x and the number of boys be y.

  2. 2

    Total students.

    x+y=10(1)x + y = 10 \qquad (1)x+y=10(1)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Girls are 4 more than boys: x=y+4x = y + 4x=y+4, that is

    x−y=4(2)x - y = 4 \qquad (2)x−y=4(2)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Table for (1), y=10−xy = 10 - xy=10−x:

    x 0 5 10
    y 10 5 0
  5. 5

    Table for (2), y=x−4y = x - 4y=x−4:

    x 4 5 6
    y 0 1 2
  6. 6

    The graph (1 cm = 1 student on both axes): line (1) falls from (0,10)(0, 10)(0,10) on the y-axis to (10,0)(10, 0)(10,0) on the x-axis. Line (2) rises from (0,−4)(0, -4)(0,−4) on the y-axis through (4,0)(4, 0)(4,0) on the x-axis. The two lines cross at one point, (7,3)(7, 3)(7,3).

  7. 7

    Read the point of intersection: x=7x = 7x=7, y=3y = 3y=3.

  8. Check: 7+3=107 + 3 = 107+3=10 ✔ and 7−3=47 - 3 = 47−3=4 ✔. In the story: 7 girls and 3 boys make 10 students, and 7 is 4 more than 3 ✔.

  9. Answer Equations x+y=10x + y = 10x+y=10 and x−y=4x - y = 4x−y=4; 7 girls and 3 boys took part.

    Common trap: Writing "girls are 4 more than boys" as x+4=yx + 4 = yx+4=y, which makes the boys the larger group. Test with numbers: if there are 3 boys, there are 3+4=73 + 4 = 73+4=7 girls, so girls === boys +4+ 4+4.
Exercise 3.1, Q1 (ii)Pencils and pens3 marks

Form the pair of linear equations in the following problems, and find their solutions graphically.
(ii) 5 pencils and 7 pens together cost ₹ 50, whereas 7 pencils and 5 pens together cost ₹ 46. Find the cost of one pencil and that of one pen.
Print graph paper

Given: two bills. Asked: a pair of equations and its graphical solution.

Concept used: forming equations, then the graphical method. Why it applies: the question asks for the solution "graphically".

  1. 1

    Let the cost of one pencil be ₹ x and the cost of one pen be ₹ y.

  2. 2

    First bill.

    5x+7y=50(1)5x + 7y = 50 \qquad (1)5x+7y=50(1)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Second bill.

    7x+5y=46(2)7x + 5y = 46 \qquad (2)7x+5y=46(2)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Table for (1), y=50−5x7y = \dfrac{50 - 5x}{7}y=750−5x​ (choose x so that y is a whole number):

    x −4 3 10
    y 10 5 0
  5. 5

    Table for (2), y=46−7x5y = \dfrac{46 - 7x}{5}y=546−7x​:

    x −2 3 8
    y 12 5 −2
  6. 6

    The graph (1 cm = 1 unit): line (1) falls gently from (−4,10)(-4, 10)(−4,10) through (3,5)(3, 5)(3,5) to (10,0)(10, 0)(10,0) on the x-axis. Line (2) falls more steeply from (−2,12)(-2, 12)(−2,12) through (3,5)(3, 5)(3,5) to (8,−2)(8, -2)(8,−2). The lines cross at (3,5)(3, 5)(3,5).

  7. 7

    Read the point of intersection: x=3x = 3x=3, y=5y = 5y=5.

  8. Check: 5(3)+7(5)=15+35=505(3) + 7(5) = 15 + 35 = 505(3)+7(5)=15+35=50 ✔ and 7(3)+5(5)=21+25=467(3) + 5(5) = 21 + 25 = 467(3)+5(5)=21+25=46 ✔.

  9. Answer Equations 5x+7y=505x + 7y = 505x+7y=50 and 7x+5y=467x + 5y = 467x+5y=46; a pencil costs ₹ 3 and a pen costs ₹ 5.

    Common trap: Choosing x=0x = 0x=0 for both tables: it gives y=507y = \dfrac{50}{7}y=750​ and y=465y = \dfrac{46}{5}y=546​, which cannot be plotted accurately. Choose x-values that make y a whole number.

The question (for all three parts of Q2): 2. On comparing the ratios a1a2\dfrac{a_1}{a_2}a2​a1​​, b1b2\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}b2​b1​​ and c1c2\dfrac{c_1}{c_2}c2​c1​​, find out whether the lines representing the following pairs of linear equations intersect at a point, are parallel or coincident:

Exercise 3.1, Q2 (i)1 mark

On comparing the ratios a1a2\dfrac{a_1}{a_2}a2​a1​​, b1b2\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}b2​b1​​ and c1c2\dfrac{c_1}{c_2}c2​c1​​, find out whether the lines representing the following pairs of linear equations intersect at a point, are parallel or coincident:
(i) 5x−4y+8=05x - 4y + 8 = 05x−4y+8=0, 7x+6y−9=07x + 6y - 9 = 07x+6y−9=0

Given: a1=5a_1 = 5a1​=5, b1=−4b_1 = -4b1​=−4, c1=8c_1 = 8c1​=8; a2=7a_2 = 7a2​=7, b2=6b_2 = 6b2​=6, c2=−9c_2 = -9c2​=−9. Asked: the type of lines.

Concept used: the ratio test (Topic 3). Why it applies: a2a_2a2​, b2b_2b2​, c2c_2c2​ are all non-zero.

  1. 1

    a1a2=57\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{5}{7}a2​a1​​=75​.

  2. 2

    b1b2=−46=−23\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{-4}{6} = -\dfrac{2}{3}b2​b1​​=6−4​=−32​.

  3. 3

    57≠−23\dfrac{5}{7} \neq -\dfrac{2}{3}75​=−32​, so the lines intersect at exactly one point.

  4. Check: one ratio is positive and the other negative, so they cannot be equal ✔.

  5. Answer The lines intersect at a point.

    Common trap: Going on to compare c1c2\dfrac{c_1}{c_2}c2​c1​​. When a1a2≠b1b2\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} \neq \dfrac{b_1}{b_2}a2​a1​​=b2​b1​​, the constants do not matter.
Exercise 3.1, Q2 (ii)1 mark

On comparing the ratios a1a2\dfrac{a_1}{a_2}a2​a1​​, b1b2\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}b2​b1​​ and c1c2\dfrac{c_1}{c_2}c2​c1​​, find out whether the lines representing the following pairs of linear equations intersect at a point, are parallel or coincident:
(ii) 9x+3y+12=09x + 3y + 12 = 09x+3y+12=0, 18x+6y+24=018x + 6y + 24 = 018x+6y+24=0

Given: a1=9a_1 = 9a1​=9, b1=3b_1 = 3b1​=3, c1=12c_1 = 12c1​=12; a2=18a_2 = 18a2​=18, b2=6b_2 = 6b2​=6, c2=24c_2 = 24c2​=24. Asked: the type of lines.

Concept used: the ratio test. Why it applies: all coefficients of the second equation are non-zero.

  1. 1

    a1a2=918=12\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{9}{18} = \dfrac{1}{2}a2​a1​​=189​=21​.

  2. 2

    b1b2=36=12\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}b2​b1​​=63​=21​.

  3. 3

    c1c2=1224=12\dfrac{c_1}{c_2} = \dfrac{12}{24} = \dfrac{1}{2}c2​c1​​=2412​=21​.

  4. 4

    All three ratios are equal, so the lines are coincident.

  5. Check: the second equation is exactly 2 times the first ✔.

  6. Answer The lines are coincident.

    Common trap: Stopping after a1a2=b1b2\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_1}{b_2}a2​a1​​=b2​b1​​ and answering "parallel". Equal first two ratios mean parallel or coincident; the third ratio decides.
Exercise 3.1, Q2 (iii)1 mark

On comparing the ratios a1a2\dfrac{a_1}{a_2}a2​a1​​, b1b2\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}b2​b1​​ and c1c2\dfrac{c_1}{c_2}c2​c1​​, find out whether the lines representing the following pairs of linear equations intersect at a point, are parallel or coincident:
(iii) 6x−3y+10=06x - 3y + 10 = 06x−3y+10=0, 2x−y+9=02x - y + 9 = 02x−y+9=0

Given: a1=6a_1 = 6a1​=6, b1=−3b_1 = -3b1​=−3, c1=10c_1 = 10c1​=10; a2=2a_2 = 2a2​=2, b2=−1b_2 = -1b2​=−1, c2=9c_2 = 9c2​=9. Asked: the type of lines.

Concept used: the ratio test. Why it applies: all coefficients of the second equation are non-zero.

  1. 1

    a1a2=62=3\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{6}{2} = 3a2​a1​​=26​=3.

  2. 2

    b1b2=−3−1=3\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{-3}{-1} = 3b2​b1​​=−1−3​=3.

  3. 3

    c1c2=109\dfrac{c_1}{c_2} = \dfrac{10}{9}c2​c1​​=910​.

  4. 4

    3=3≠1093 = 3 \neq \dfrac{10}{9}3=3=910​, so the lines are parallel.

  5. Check: 3 times the second equation is 6x−3y+27=06x - 3y + 27 = 06x−3y+27=0, with the same x- and y-parts as the first but a different constant ✔.

  6. Answer The lines are parallel.

    Common trap: Writing b1b2=−3−1=−3\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{-3}{-1} = -3b2​b1​​=−1−3​=−3. A negative divided by a negative is positive.

The question (for all five parts of Q3): 3. On comparing the ratios a1a2\dfrac{a_1}{a_2}a2​a1​​, b1b2\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}b2​b1​​ and c1c2\dfrac{c_1}{c_2}c2​c1​​, find out whether the following pair of linear equations are consistent, or inconsistent.

Exercise 3.1, Q3 (i)1 mark

On comparing the ratios a1a2\dfrac{a_1}{a_2}a2​a1​​, b1b2\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}b2​b1​​ and c1c2\dfrac{c_1}{c_2}c2​c1​​, find out whether the following pair of linear equations are consistent, or inconsistent.
(i) 3x+2y=53x + 2y = 53x+2y=5 ; 2x−3y=72x - 3y = 72x−3y=7

Given: a1=3a_1 = 3a1​=3, b1=2b_1 = 2b1​=2; a2=2a_2 = 2a2​=2, b2=−3b_2 = -3b2​=−3. Asked: consistent or inconsistent.

Concept used: the ratio test; consistent = at least one solution. Why it applies: the coefficients decide the number of solutions.

  1. 1

    a1a2=32\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{3}{2}a2​a1​​=23​.

  2. 2

    b1b2=2−3=−23\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{2}{-3} = -\dfrac{2}{3}b2​b1​​=−32​=−32​.

  3. 3

    32≠−23\dfrac{3}{2} \neq -\dfrac{2}{3}23​=−32​: the lines intersect, so there is exactly one solution.

  4. Check: solving gives x=2913x = \dfrac{29}{13}x=1329​, y=−1113y = -\dfrac{11}{13}y=−1311​ — one solution exists ✔.

  5. Answer Consistent (unique solution).

    Common trap: Thinking "consistent" means "infinitely many". Consistent means "has a solution" — one, or infinitely many.
Exercise 3.1, Q3 (ii)1 mark

On comparing the ratios a1a2\dfrac{a_1}{a_2}a2​a1​​, b1b2\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}b2​b1​​ and c1c2\dfrac{c_1}{c_2}c2​c1​​, find out whether the following pair of linear equations are consistent, or inconsistent.
(ii) 2x−3y=82x - 3y = 82x−3y=8 ; 4x−6y=94x - 6y = 94x−6y=9

Given: a1=2a_1 = 2a1​=2, b1=−3b_1 = -3b1​=−3, c1=−8c_1 = -8c1​=−8; a2=4a_2 = 4a2​=4, b2=−6b_2 = -6b2​=−6, c2=−9c_2 = -9c2​=−9 (both written as ax+by+c=0ax + by + c = 0ax+by+c=0). Asked: consistent or inconsistent.

Concept used: the ratio test, both equations in the same form. Why it applies: the first two ratios turn out equal, so the constants matter.

  1. 1

    a1a2=24=12\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}a2​a1​​=42​=21​.

  2. 2

    b1b2=−3−6=12\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{-3}{-6} = \dfrac{1}{2}b2​b1​​=−6−3​=21​.

  3. 3

    c1c2=−8−9=89\dfrac{c_1}{c_2} = \dfrac{-8}{-9} = \dfrac{8}{9}c2​c1​​=−9−8​=98​.

  4. 4

    12=12≠89\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \neq \dfrac{8}{9}21​=21​=98​: parallel lines, no solution.

  5. Check: doubling the first equation gives 4x−6y=164x - 6y = 164x−6y=16; the second says 4x−6y=94x - 6y = 94x−6y=9. The same expression cannot equal 16 and 9 ✔.

  6. Answer Inconsistent.

    Common trap: Taking c1=8c_1 = 8c1​=8 from "=8= 8=8" but c2=−9c_2 = -9c2​=−9 from a general form — mixing forms changes the sign of c1c2\dfrac{c_1}{c_2}c2​c1​​.
Exercise 3.1, Q3 (iii)1 mark

On comparing the ratios a1a2\dfrac{a_1}{a_2}a2​a1​​, b1b2\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}b2​b1​​ and c1c2\dfrac{c_1}{c_2}c2​c1​​, find out whether the following pair of linear equations are consistent, or inconsistent.
(iii) 32x+53y=7\dfrac{3}{2}x + \dfrac{5}{3}y = 723​x+35​y=7 ; 9x−10y=149x - 10y = 149x−10y=14

Given: a1=32a_1 = \dfrac{3}{2}a1​=23​, b1=53b_1 = \dfrac{5}{3}b1​=35​; a2=9a_2 = 9a2​=9, b2=−10b_2 = -10b2​=−10. Asked: consistent or inconsistent.

Concept used: the ratio test with fractions. Why it applies: a2a_2a2​ and b2b_2b2​ are non-zero.

  1. 1

    a1a2=32÷9=318=16\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{3}{2} \div 9 = \dfrac{3}{18} = \dfrac{1}{6}a2​a1​​=23​÷9=183​=61​.

  2. 2

    b1b2=53÷(−10)=−530=−16\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{5}{3} \div (-10) = -\dfrac{5}{30} = -\dfrac{1}{6}b2​b1​​=35​÷(−10)=−305​=−61​.

  3. 3

    16≠−16\dfrac{1}{6} \neq -\dfrac{1}{6}61​=−61​: the lines intersect — one solution.

  4. Check: multiplying the first equation by 6 gives 9x+10y=429x + 10y = 429x+10y=42. With 9x−10y=149x - 10y = 149x−10y=14, adding gives 18x=5618x = 5618x=56 — a single value of x, so one solution ✔.

  5. Answer Consistent.

    Common trap: Dropping the minus sign of −10-10−10 and concluding the ratios are equal (both 16\dfrac{1}{6}61​), which would wrongly suggest parallel or coincident lines.
Exercise 3.1, Q3 (iv)1 mark

On comparing the ratios a1a2\dfrac{a_1}{a_2}a2​a1​​, b1b2\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}b2​b1​​ and c1c2\dfrac{c_1}{c_2}c2​c1​​, find out whether the following pair of linear equations are consistent, or inconsistent.
(iv) 5x−3y=115x - 3y = 115x−3y=11 ; −10x+6y=−22-10x + 6y = -22−10x+6y=−22

Given: a1=5a_1 = 5a1​=5, b1=−3b_1 = -3b1​=−3, c1=−11c_1 = -11c1​=−11; a2=−10a_2 = -10a2​=−10, b2=6b_2 = 6b2​=6, c2=22c_2 = 22c2​=22. Asked: consistent or inconsistent.

Concept used: the ratio test. Why it applies: all coefficients of the second equation are non-zero.

  1. 1

    a1a2=5−10=−12\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{5}{-10} = -\dfrac{1}{2}a2​a1​​=−105​=−21​.

  2. 2

    b1b2=−36=−12\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{-3}{6} = -\dfrac{1}{2}b2​b1​​=6−3​=−21​.

  3. 3

    c1c2=−1122=−12\dfrac{c_1}{c_2} = \dfrac{-11}{22} = -\dfrac{1}{2}c2​c1​​=22−11​=−21​.

  4. 4

    All three are equal: coincident lines, infinitely many solutions.

  5. Check: the second equation is −2-2−2 times the first ✔.

  6. Answer Consistent (dependent — infinitely many solutions).

    Common trap: Answering "inconsistent" because there is no single answer. Infinitely many solutions is still consistent.
Exercise 3.1, Q3 (v)1 mark

On comparing the ratios a1a2\dfrac{a_1}{a_2}a2​a1​​, b1b2\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}b2​b1​​ and c1c2\dfrac{c_1}{c_2}c2​c1​​, find out whether the following pair of linear equations are consistent, or inconsistent.
(v) 43x+2y=8\dfrac{4}{3}x + 2y = 834​x+2y=8 ; 2x+3y=122x + 3y = 122x+3y=12

Given: a1=43a_1 = \dfrac{4}{3}a1​=34​, b1=2b_1 = 2b1​=2, c1=−8c_1 = -8c1​=−8; a2=2a_2 = 2a2​=2, b2=3b_2 = 3b2​=3, c2=−12c_2 = -12c2​=−12. Asked: consistent or inconsistent.

Concept used: the ratio test. Why it applies: all coefficients of the second equation are non-zero.

  1. 1

    a1a2=43÷2=23\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{4}{3} \div 2 = \dfrac{2}{3}a2​a1​​=34​÷2=32​.

  2. 2

    b1b2=23\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{2}{3}b2​b1​​=32​.

  3. 3

    c1c2=−8−12=23\dfrac{c_1}{c_2} = \dfrac{-8}{-12} = \dfrac{2}{3}c2​c1​​=−12−8​=32​.

  4. 4

    All three are equal: coincident lines, infinitely many solutions.

  5. Check: multiplying 2x+3y=122x + 3y = 122x+3y=12 by 23\dfrac{2}{3}32​ gives 43x+2y=8\dfrac{4}{3}x + 2y = 834​x+2y=8 ✔.

  6. Answer Consistent (dependent — infinitely many solutions).

    Common trap: Computing 43÷2\dfrac{4}{3} \div 234​÷2 as 83\dfrac{8}{3}38​ (multiplying instead of dividing).

The question (for all four parts of Q4): 4. Which of the following pairs of linear equations are consistent/inconsistent? If consistent, obtain the solution graphically:

Exercise 3.1, Q4 (i)3 marks

Which of the following pairs of linear equations are consistent/inconsistent? If consistent, obtain the solution graphically:
(i) x+y=5x + y = 5x+y=5, 2x+2y=102x + 2y = 102x+2y=10
Print graph paper

Given: x+y=5x + y = 5x+y=5 and 2x+2y=102x + 2y = 102x+2y=10. Asked: consistent or not; if so, the solution from a graph.

Concept used: the ratio test, then the graph. Why it applies: the ratios tell us what the graph will show.

  1. 1

    Ratios: 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​, 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​, −5−10=12\dfrac{-5}{-10} = \dfrac{1}{2}−10−5​=21​ — all equal. The pair is consistent (dependent).

  2. 2

    Table for x+y=5x + y = 5x+y=5:

    x 0 2 5
    y 5 3 0
  3. 3

    Table for 2x+2y=102x + 2y = 102x+2y=10: the same points satisfy it, e.g. 2(2)+2(3)=102(2) + 2(3) = 102(2)+2(3)=10.

  4. 4

    The graph: both equations give one and the same line through (0,5)(0, 5)(0,5), (2,3)(2, 3)(2,3) and (5,0)(5, 0)(5,0). The lines are coincident.

  5. 5

    Every point of this line is a solution: y=5−xy = 5 - xy=5−x, for any value of x.

  6. Check: (1,4)(1, 4)(1,4) and (4,1)(4, 1)(4,1) satisfy both equations: 1+4=51 + 4 = 51+4=5, 2+8=102 + 8 = 102+8=10; 4+1=54 + 1 = 54+1=5, 8+2=108 + 2 = 108+2=10 ✔.

  7. Answer Consistent, with infinitely many solutions: every (x,y)(x, y)(x,y) with y=5−xy = 5 - xy=5−x (the lines coincide).

    Common trap: Giving just one point, such as (2,3)(2, 3)(2,3), as "the solution". Here every point of the line is a solution.
Exercise 3.1, Q4 (ii)2 marks

Which of the following pairs of linear equations are consistent/inconsistent? If consistent, obtain the solution graphically:
(ii) x−y=8x - y = 8x−y=8, 3x−3y=163x - 3y = 163x−3y=16

Given: x−y=8x - y = 8x−y=8 and 3x−3y=163x - 3y = 163x−3y=16. Asked: consistent or not.

Concept used: the ratio test. Why it applies: a graph is needed only if the pair is consistent.

  1. 1

    a1a2=13\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{1}{3}a2​a1​​=31​, b1b2=−1−3=13\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{-1}{-3} = \dfrac{1}{3}b2​b1​​=−3−1​=31​.

  2. 2

    c1c2=−8−16=12\dfrac{c_1}{c_2} = \dfrac{-8}{-16} = \dfrac{1}{2}c2​c1​​=−16−8​=21​.

  3. 3

    13=13≠12\dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \neq \dfrac{1}{2}31​=31​=21​: parallel lines, no solution.

  4. Check: 3 times the first gives 3x−3y=243x - 3y = 243x−3y=24, but the second says 3x−3y=163x - 3y = 163x−3y=16 ✔. (If drawn, the lines y=x−8y = x - 8y=x−8 and y=x−163y = x - \dfrac{16}{3}y=x−316​ are parallel.)

  5. Answer Inconsistent — no solution, so there is nothing to read from a graph.

    Common trap: Drawing the graph anyway and reading a "meeting point" where two nearly-touching lines seem to cross. Parallel lines never meet.
Exercise 3.1, Q4 (iii)3 marks

Which of the following pairs of linear equations are consistent/inconsistent? If consistent, obtain the solution graphically:
(iii) 2x+y−6=02x + y - 6 = 02x+y−6=0, 4x−2y−4=04x - 2y - 4 = 04x−2y−4=0
Print graph paper

Given: 2x+y−6=02x + y - 6 = 02x+y−6=0 and 4x−2y−4=04x - 2y - 4 = 04x−2y−4=0. Asked: consistent or not; if so, the solution from a graph.

Concept used: the ratio test, then the graphical method. Why it applies: the ratios show one solution, which the graph then finds.

  1. 1

    a1a2=24=12\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}a2​a1​​=42​=21​, b1b2=1−2=−12\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{1}{-2} = -\dfrac{1}{2}b2​b1​​=−21​=−21​. Not equal: consistent, one solution.

  2. 2

    Table for 2x+y=62x + y = 62x+y=6, i.e. y=6−2xy = 6 - 2xy=6−2x:

    x 0 2 3
    y 6 2 0
  3. 3

    Table for 4x−2y=44x - 2y = 44x−2y=4, i.e. y=2x−2y = 2x - 2y=2x−2:

    x 0 1 2
    y −2 0 2
  4. 4

    The graph (1 cm = 1 unit): the first line falls from (0,6)(0, 6)(0,6) to (3,0)(3, 0)(3,0); the second rises from (0,−2)(0, -2)(0,−2) through (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0). They cross at (2,2)(2, 2)(2,2).

  5. 5

    Read the point of intersection: x=2x = 2x=2, y=2y = 2y=2.

  6. Check: 2(2)+2−6=02(2) + 2 - 6 = 02(2)+2−6=0 ✔ and 4(2)−2(2)−4=04(2) - 2(2) - 4 = 04(2)−2(2)−4=0 ✔.

  7. Answer Consistent; the solution is x=2x = 2x=2, y=2y = 2y=2.

    Common trap: Making y the subject of 4x−2y−4=04x - 2y - 4 = 04x−2y−4=0 as y=2−2xy = 2 - 2xy=2−2x. From −2y=4−4x-2y = 4 - 4x−2y=4−4x, dividing every term by −2-2−2 gives y=2x−2y = 2x - 2y=2x−2.
Exercise 3.1, Q4 (iv)2 marks

Which of the following pairs of linear equations are consistent/inconsistent? If consistent, obtain the solution graphically:
(iv) 2x−2y−2=02x - 2y - 2 = 02x−2y−2=0, 4x−4y−5=04x - 4y - 5 = 04x−4y−5=0

Given: 2x−2y−2=02x - 2y - 2 = 02x−2y−2=0 and 4x−4y−5=04x - 4y - 5 = 04x−4y−5=0. Asked: consistent or not.

Concept used: the ratio test. Why it applies: a graph is needed only if the pair is consistent.

  1. 1

    a1a2=24=12\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}a2​a1​​=42​=21​, b1b2=−2−4=12\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{-2}{-4} = \dfrac{1}{2}b2​b1​​=−4−2​=21​.

  2. 2

    c1c2=−2−5=25\dfrac{c_1}{c_2} = \dfrac{-2}{-5} = \dfrac{2}{5}c2​c1​​=−5−2​=52​.

  3. 3

    12=12≠25\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \neq \dfrac{2}{5}21​=21​=52​: parallel lines, no solution.

  4. Check: the first equation gives x−y=1x - y = 1x−y=1; the second gives x−y=54x - y = \dfrac{5}{4}x−y=45​. Both cannot hold ✔.

  5. Answer Inconsistent — no solution.

    Common trap: Simplifying −2−5\dfrac{-2}{-5}−5−2​ to −25-\dfrac{2}{5}−52​. The two minus signs cancel.
Exercise 3.1, Q5The rectangular garden3 marks
  1. Half the perimeter of a rectangular garden, whose length is 4 m more than its width, is 36 m. Find the dimensions of the garden.
    Print graph paper

Given: length = width + 4; half the perimeter = 36 m. Asked: the length and the width.

Concept used: form the pair (Topic 6) and solve it graphically, as in this exercise (Topic 2). Why it applies: half the perimeter of a rectangle is length + width.

  1. 1

    Let the length be x m and the width be y m.

  2. 2

    Half the perimeter.

    x+y=36(1)x + y = 36 \qquad (1)x+y=36(1)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Length is 4 m more than width: x=y+4x = y + 4x=y+4, that is

    x−y=4(2)x - y = 4 \qquad (2)x−y=4(2)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Table for (1):

    x 0 20 36
    y 36 16 0
  5. 5

    Table for (2), y=x−4y = x - 4y=x−4:

    x 4 20 24
    y 0 16 20
  6. 6

    The graph (1 cm = 4 m on both axes): line (1) falls from (0,36)(0, 36)(0,36) to (36,0)(36, 0)(36,0); line (2) rises from (4,0)(4, 0)(4,0) through (24,20)(24, 20)(24,20). They cross at (20,16)(20, 16)(20,16).

  7. 7

    Read the point of intersection: x=20x = 20x=20, y=16y = 16y=16.

  8. Check: 20+16=3620 + 16 = 3620+16=36 ✔ and 20=16+420 = 16 + 420=16+4 ✔. Full perimeter 2(20+16)=722(20 + 16) = 722(20+16)=72 m, half of it 36 m ✔.

  9. Answer Length 20 m, width 16 m.

    Common trap: Writing 2(x+y)=362(x + y) = 362(x+y)=36. The question gives half the perimeter, which is x+yx + yx+y.

The question (for all three parts of Q6): 6. Given the linear equation 2x+3y−8=02x + 3y - 8 = 02x+3y−8=0, write another linear equation in two variables such that the geometrical representation of the pair so formed is: (i) intersecting lines (ii) parallel lines (iii) coincident lines

Exercise 3.1, Q6 (i)Intersecting lines1 mark

Given the linear equation 2x+3y−8=02x + 3y - 8 = 02x+3y−8=0, write another linear equation in two variables such that the geometrical representation of the pair so formed is:
(i) intersecting lines

Given: a1=2a_1 = 2a1​=2, b1=3b_1 = 3b1​=3, c1=−8c_1 = -8c1​=−8. Asked: a second equation giving intersecting lines.

Concept used: intersecting ⇔ a1a2≠b1b2\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} \neq \dfrac{b_1}{b_2}a2​a1​​=b2​b1​​. Why it applies: we choose a2a_2a2​ and b2b_2b2​ so that the ratios differ.

  1. 1

    Choose a2=3a_2 = 3a2​=3 and b2=−1b_2 = -1b2​=−1, with any constant, say −2-2−2: the equation 3x−y−2=03x - y - 2 = 03x−y−2=0.

  2. 2

    a1a2=23\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{2}{3}a2​a1​​=32​ and b1b2=3−1=−3\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{3}{-1} = -3b2​b1​​=−13​=−3. They differ.

  3. Check: solving the pair: y=3x−2y = 3x - 2y=3x−2 gives 2x+9x−6=82x + 9x - 6 = 82x+9x−6=8, so x=1411x = \dfrac{14}{11}x=1114​ — exactly one point ✔.

  4. Answer For example, 3x−y−2=03x - y - 2 = 03x−y−2=0. (Any equation with a1a2≠b1b2\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} \neq \dfrac{b_1}{b_2}a2​a1​​=b2​b1​​ is correct.)

    Common trap: Choosing coefficients in the same ratio, such as 4x+6y−1=04x + 6y - 1 = 04x+6y−1=0, which gives parallel lines.
Exercise 3.1, Q6 (ii)Parallel lines1 mark

Given the linear equation 2x+3y−8=02x + 3y - 8 = 02x+3y−8=0, write another linear equation in two variables such that the geometrical representation of the pair so formed is:
(ii) parallel lines

Given: a1=2a_1 = 2a1​=2, b1=3b_1 = 3b1​=3, c1=−8c_1 = -8c1​=−8. Asked: a second equation giving parallel lines.

Concept used: parallel ⇔ a1a2=b1b2≠c1c2\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_1}{b_2} \neq \dfrac{c_1}{c_2}a2​a1​​=b2​b1​​=c2​c1​​. Why it applies: we multiply only the x- and y-parts by the same number.

  1. 1

    Multiply the x- and y-parts by 2: 4x+6y4x + 6y4x+6y. Choose a constant that is not 2×(−8)=−162 \times (-8) = -162×(−8)=−16, say +5+5+5.

  2. 2

    The equation 4x+6y+5=04x + 6y + 5 = 04x+6y+5=0: ratios 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​, 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​, −85\dfrac{-8}{5}5−8​.

  3. Check: 12=12≠−85\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \neq -\dfrac{8}{5}21​=21​=−58​ ✔ — parallel.

  4. Answer For example, 4x+6y+5=04x + 6y + 5 = 04x+6y+5=0.

    Common trap: Doubling the constant too (4x+6y−16=04x + 6y - 16 = 04x+6y−16=0): that is the same line.
Exercise 3.1, Q6 (iii)Coincident lines1 mark

Given the linear equation 2x+3y−8=02x + 3y - 8 = 02x+3y−8=0, write another linear equation in two variables such that the geometrical representation of the pair so formed is:
(iii) coincident lines

Given: a1=2a_1 = 2a1​=2, b1=3b_1 = 3b1​=3, c1=−8c_1 = -8c1​=−8. Asked: a second equation giving the same line.

Concept used: coincident ⇔ all three ratios equal. Why it applies: multiplying the whole equation by a non-zero number keeps the line.

  1. 1

    Multiply every term by 3: 6x+9y−24=06x + 9y - 24 = 06x+9y−24=0.

  2. 2

    Ratios: 26=13\dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}62​=31​, 39=13\dfrac{3}{9} = \dfrac{1}{3}93​=31​, −8−24=13\dfrac{-8}{-24} = \dfrac{1}{3}−24−8​=31​.

  3. Check: all three ratios equal ✔; e.g. (4,0)(4, 0)(4,0) is on both lines: 8−8=08 - 8 = 08−8=0 and 24−24=024 - 24 = 024−24=0 ✔.

  4. Answer For example, 6x+9y−24=06x + 9y - 24 = 06x+9y−24=0.

    Common trap: Multiplying the x- and y-terms but forgetting the constant.
Exercise 3.1, Q7A triangle with the x-axis4 marks
  1. Draw the graphs of the equations x−y+1=0x - y + 1 = 0x−y+1=0 and 3x+2y−12=03x + 2y - 12 = 03x+2y−12=0. Determine the coordinates of the vertices of the triangle formed by these lines and the x-axis, and shade the triangular region.
    Print graph paper

Given: two lines. Asked: their graphs; the vertices of the triangle they make with the x-axis; shading.

Concept used: the graphical method; the triangle's vertices are the meeting point and the two x-intercepts (Topic 2). Why it applies: the triangle is bounded by the two lines and the x-axis.

  1. 1

    Table for x−y+1=0x - y + 1 = 0x−y+1=0, i.e. y=x+1y = x + 1y=x+1:

    x −1 0 2
    y 0 1 3
  2. 2

    Table for 3x+2y−12=03x + 2y - 12 = 03x+2y−12=0, i.e. y=12−3x2y = \dfrac{12 - 3x}{2}y=212−3x​:

    x 0 2 4
    y 6 3 0
  3. 3

    The graph (1 cm = 1 unit): the first line rises from (−1,0)(-1, 0)(−1,0) on the x-axis through (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1); the second falls from (0,6)(0, 6)(0,6) to (4,0)(4, 0)(4,0) on the x-axis. They cross at (2,3)(2, 3)(2,3).

  4. 4

    The vertices of the triangle: the meeting point (2,3)(2, 3)(2,3) and the two points on the x-axis, (−1,0)(-1, 0)(−1,0) and (4,0)(4, 0)(4,0).

    Shade the region inside these three points: above the x-axis, below both lines.

  7. Answer Vertices (−1,0)(-1, 0)(−1,0), (4,0)(4, 0)(4,0) and (2,3)(2, 3)(2,3). (If the area is also asked: base =4−(−1)=5= 4 - (-1) = 5=4−(−1)=5, height =3= 3=3, area =12×5×3=7.5= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 3 = 7.5=21​×5×3=7.5 square units.)

Exercise 3.2

The question (for all six parts of Q1): 1. Solve the following pair of linear equations by the substitution method.

Exercise 3.2, Q1 (i)2 marks

Solve the following pair of linear equations by the substitution method.
(i) x+y=14x + y = 14x+y=14, x−y=4x - y = 4x−y=4

Given: x+y=14x + y = 14x+y=14 and x−y=4x - y = 4x−y=4. Asked: x and y, by substitution.

Concept used: the substitution routine (Topic 4). Why it applies: x has coefficient 1 in both equations.

  1. 1

    From x−y=4x - y = 4x−y=4, add y to both sides.

    x=y+4x = y + 4x=y+4Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Substitute into x+y=14x + y = 14x+y=14.

    (y+4)+y=14(y + 4) + y = 14(y+4)+y=14Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Collect the y-terms.

    2y+4=142y + 4 = 142y+4=14Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Subtract 4 from both sides.

    2y=102y = 102y=10Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Divide by 2.

    y=5y = 5y=5Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Back-substitute into x=y+4x = y + 4x=y+4.

    x=9x = 9x=9Swipe to see the whole equation →

  7. Check: 9+5=149 + 5 = 149+5=14 ✔ and 9−5=49 - 5 = 49−5=4 ✔.

  8. Answer x=9x = 9x=9, y=5y = 5y=5

    Common trap: Substituting x=y+4x = y + 4x=y+4 back into x−y=4x - y = 4x−y=4, the equation it came from. That gives 4=44 = 44=4 and no value of y.
Exercise 3.2, Q1 (ii)2 marks

Solve the following pair of linear equations by the substitution method.
(ii) s−t=3s - t = 3s−t=3, s3+t2=6\dfrac{s}{3} + \dfrac{t}{2} = 63s​+2t​=6

Given: s−t=3s - t = 3s−t=3 and s3+t2=6\dfrac{s}{3} + \dfrac{t}{2} = 63s​+2t​=6. Asked: s and t.

Concept used: clear fractions, then substitution. Why it applies: s has coefficient 1 in the first equation.

  1. 1

    Multiply every term of the second equation by 6 (the LCM of 3 and 2).

    2s+3t=362s + 3t = 362s+3t=36Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    From s−t=3s - t = 3s−t=3, add t to both sides.

    s=t+3s = t + 3s=t+3Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Substitute into 2s+3t=362s + 3t = 362s+3t=36.

    2(t+3)+3t=362(t + 3) + 3t = 362(t+3)+3t=36Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Expand the bracket.

    2t+6+3t=362t + 6 + 3t = 362t+6+3t=36Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Collect the t-terms.

    5t+6=365t + 6 = 365t+6=36Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Subtract 6 from both sides.

    5t=305t = 305t=30Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Divide by 5.

    t=6t = 6t=6Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Back-substitute into s=t+3s = t + 3s=t+3.

    s=9s = 9s=9Swipe to see the whole equation →

  9. Check: 9−6=39 - 6 = 39−6=3 ✔ and 93+62=3+3=6\dfrac{9}{3} + \dfrac{6}{2} = 3 + 3 = 639​+26​=3+3=6 ✔.

  10. Answer s=9s = 9s=9, t=6t = 6t=6

    Common trap: Multiplying by 6 but leaving the right side as 6 (2s+3t=62s + 3t = 62s+3t=6). Every term, including the 6, is multiplied.
Exercise 3.2, Q1 (iii)2 marks

Solve the following pair of linear equations by the substitution method.
(iii) 3x−y=33x - y = 33x−y=3, 9x−3y=99x - 3y = 99x−3y=9

Given: 3x−y=33x - y = 33x−y=3 and 9x−3y=99x - 3y = 99x−3y=9. Asked: the solution(s).

Concept used: substitution; a true statement with no variable means infinitely many solutions. Why it applies: y has coefficient −1-1−1 in the first equation.

  1. 1

    From 3x−y=33x - y = 33x−y=3, add y to both sides.

    3x=3+y3x = 3 + y3x=3+ySwipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Subtract 3 from both sides.

    y=3x−3y = 3x - 3y=3x−3Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Substitute into 9x−3y=99x - 3y = 99x−3y=9.

    9x−3(3x−3)=99x - 3(3x - 3) = 99x−3(3x−3)=9Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Expand the bracket.

    9x−9x+9=99x - 9x + 9 = 99x−9x+9=9Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Collect the x-terms.

    9=99 = 99=9Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    This is true for every x: the pair has infinitely many solutions — every pair with y=3x−3y = 3x - 3y=3x−3.

  7. Check: the second equation is 3 times the first (ratios 13\dfrac{1}{3}31​, 13\dfrac{1}{3}31​, 13\dfrac{1}{3}31​) — coincident lines ✔. For example (2,3)(2, 3)(2,3): 6−3=36 - 3 = 36−3=3 ✔, 18−9=918 - 9 = 918−9=9 ✔.

  8. Answer Infinitely many solutions: y=3x−3y = 3x - 3y=3x−3, where x can be any real number.

    Common trap: Writing "9=99 = 99=9, so x=9x = 9x=9" or "no solution". A true statement with no variable means infinitely many solutions.
Exercise 3.2, Q1 (iv)2 marks

Solve the following pair of linear equations by the substitution method.
(iv) 0.2x+0.3y=1.30.2x + 0.3y = 1.30.2x+0.3y=1.3, 0.4x+0.5y=2.30.4x + 0.5y = 2.30.4x+0.5y=2.3

Given: two equations with decimals. Asked: x and y.

Concept used: clear decimals, then substitution. Why it applies: whole-number coefficients are safer.

  1. 1

    Multiply every term of the first equation by 10.

    2x+3y=132x + 3y = 132x+3y=13Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Multiply every term of the second equation by 10.

    4x+5y=234x + 5y = 234x+5y=23Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    From 2x+3y=132x + 3y = 132x+3y=13, subtract 3y3y3y from both sides.

    2x=13−3y2x = 13 - 3y2x=13−3ySwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Divide by 2.

    x=13−3y2x = \dfrac{13 - 3y}{2}x=213−3y​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Substitute into 4x+5y=234x + 5y = 234x+5y=23.

    4×13−3y2+5y=234 \times \dfrac{13 - 3y}{2} + 5y = 234×213−3y​+5y=23Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Simplify: 4÷2=24 \div 2 = 24÷2=2.

    2(13−3y)+5y=232(13 - 3y) + 5y = 232(13−3y)+5y=23Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Expand the bracket.

    26−6y+5y=2326 - 6y + 5y = 2326−6y+5y=23Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Collect the y-terms.

    26−y=2326 - y = 2326−y=23Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    Subtract 26 from both sides.

    −y=−3-y = -3−y=−3Swipe to see the whole equation →
  10. 10

    Multiply both sides by −1-1−1.

    y=3y = 3y=3Swipe to see the whole equation →
  11. 11

    Back-substitute into x=13−3y2x = \dfrac{13 - 3y}{2}x=213−3y​.

    x=13−92=2x = \dfrac{13 - 9}{2} = 2x=213−9​=2Swipe to see the whole equation →

  12. Check: 0.2(2)+0.3(3)=0.4+0.9=1.30.2(2) + 0.3(3) = 0.4 + 0.9 = 1.30.2(2)+0.3(3)=0.4+0.9=1.3 ✔ and 0.4(2)+0.5(3)=0.8+1.5=2.30.4(2) + 0.5(3) = 0.8 + 1.5 = 2.30.4(2)+0.5(3)=0.8+1.5=2.3 ✔.

  13. Answer x=2x = 2x=2, y=3y = 3y=3

    Common trap: Multiplying the decimals by 10 on the left but not the right (2x+3y=1.32x + 3y = 1.32x+3y=1.3).
Exercise 3.2, Q1 (v)2 marks

Solve the following pair of linear equations by the substitution method.
(v) 2 x+3 y=0\sqrt{2}\,x + \sqrt{3}\,y = 02​x+3​y=0, 3 x−8 y=0\sqrt{3}\,x - \sqrt{8}\,y = 03​x−8​y=0

Given: two equations with surd coefficients and zero constants. Asked: x and y.

Concept used: substitution; 8=22\sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}8​=22​. Why it applies: the routine works with any real coefficients.

  1. 1

    From the first equation, subtract 3 y\sqrt{3}\,y3​y from both sides.

    2 x=−3 y\sqrt{2}\,x = -\sqrt{3}\,y2​x=−3​ySwipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Divide by 2\sqrt{2}2​.

    x=−32 yx = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}}\,yx=−2​3​​ySwipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Substitute into 3 x−8 y=0\sqrt{3}\,x - \sqrt{8}\,y = 03​x−8​y=0.

    3(−32 y)−8 y=0\sqrt{3}\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}}\,y\right) - \sqrt{8}\,y = 03​(−2​3​​y)−8​y=0Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Use 3×3=3\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} = 33​×3​=3 and 8=22\sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}8​=22​.

    −32 y−22 y=0-\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\,y - 2\sqrt{2}\,y = 0−2​3​y−22​y=0Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Multiply every term by 2\sqrt{2}2​ (and 22×2=42\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{2} = 422​×2​=4).

    −3y−4y=0-3y - 4y = 0−3y−4y=0Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Collect the y-terms.

    −7y=0-7y = 0−7y=0Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Divide by −7-7−7.

    y=0y = 0y=0Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Back-substitute into x=−32 yx = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}}\,yx=−2​3​​y.

    x=0x = 0x=0Swipe to see the whole equation →

  9. Check: (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0) satisfies both equations ✔. It is the only solution: a1a2=23\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}a2​a1​​=3​2​​ is positive and b1b2=3−8\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{-\sqrt{8}}b2​b1​​=−8​3​​ is negative, so they differ ✔.

  10. Answer x=0x = 0x=0, y=0y = 0y=0

    Common trap: Seeing "=0= 0=0" on both right sides and deciding the lines are the same. Both lines pass through the origin, but they are different lines meeting only there.
Exercise 3.2, Q1 (vi)2 marks

Solve the following pair of linear equations by the substitution method.
(vi) 3x2−5y3=−2\dfrac{3x}{2} - \dfrac{5y}{3} = -223x​−35y​=−2, x3+y2=136\dfrac{x}{3} + \dfrac{y}{2} = \dfrac{13}{6}3x​+2y​=613​

Given: two equations with fractions. Asked: x and y.

Concept used: clear fractions, then substitution. Why it applies: multiplying by 6 removes every denominator.

    Multiply every term of the first equation by 6.

  6. 6

    Multiply every term by 2.

    9(13−3y)−20y=−249(13 - 3y) - 20y = -249(13−3y)−20y=−24Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Expand the bracket.

    117−27y−20y=−24117 - 27y - 20y = -24117−27y−20y=−24Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Collect the y-terms.

    117−47y=−24117 - 47y = -24117−47y=−24Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    Subtract 117 from both sides.

    −47y=−141-47y = -141−47y=−141Swipe to see the whole equation →

    Divide by −47-47−47.

    y=3y = 3y=3Swipe to see the whole equation →
  11. 11

    Back-substitute into x=13−3y2x = \dfrac{13 - 3y}{2}x=213−3y​.

    x=13−92=2x = \dfrac{13 - 9}{2} = 2x=213−9​=2Swipe to see the whole equation →

  12. Check: 3(2)2−5(3)3=3−5=−2\dfrac{3(2)}{2} - \dfrac{5(3)}{3} = 3 - 5 = -223(2)​−35(3)​=3−5=−2 ✔ and 23+32=4+96=136\dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{3}{2} = \dfrac{4 + 9}{6} = \dfrac{13}{6}32​+23​=64+9​=613​ ✔.

  13. Answer x=2x = 2x=2, y=3y = 3y=3

Exercise 3.2, Q2Solve, then find m3 marks
  1. Solve 2x+3y=112x + 3y = 112x+3y=11 and 2x−4y=−242x - 4y = -242x−4y=−24 and hence find the value of 'm' for which y=mx+3y = mx + 3y=mx+3.

Given: a pair of equations; the solution lies on y=mx+3y = mx + 3y=mx+3. Asked: x, y and m.

Concept used: substitution; then substitute the solution into y=mx+3y = mx + 3y=mx+3. Why it applies: the point (x,y)(x, y)(x,y) found must satisfy the third equation.

  1. 1

    From 2x+3y=112x + 3y = 112x+3y=11, subtract 3y3y3y from both sides.

    2x=11−3y2x = 11 - 3y2x=11−3ySwipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Substitute 2x=11−3y2x = 11 - 3y2x=11−3y into 2x−4y=−242x - 4y = -242x−4y=−24.

    (11−3y)−4y=−24(11 - 3y) - 4y = -24(11−3y)−4y=−24Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Collect the y-terms.

    11−7y=−2411 - 7y = -2411−7y=−24Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Subtract 11 from both sides.

    −7y=−35-7y = -35−7y=−35Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Divide by −7-7−7.

    y=5y = 5y=5Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Back-substitute into 2x=11−3y2x = 11 - 3y2x=11−3y.

    2x=11−15=−42x = 11 - 15 = -42x=11−15=−4Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Divide by 2.

    x=−2x = -2x=−2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Put x=−2x = -2x=−2, y=5y = 5y=5 into y=mx+3y = mx + 3y=mx+3.

    5=−2m+35 = -2m + 35=−2m+3Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    Subtract 3 from both sides.

    2=−2m2 = -2m2=−2mSwipe to see the whole equation →

    Divide by −2-2−2.

    m=−1m = -1m=−1Swipe to see the whole equation →

  11. Check: 2(−2)+3(5)=−4+15=112(-2) + 3(5) = -4 + 15 = 112(−2)+3(5)=−4+15=11 ✔; 2(−2)−4(5)=−4−20=−242(-2) - 4(5) = -4 - 20 = -242(−2)−4(5)=−4−20=−24 ✔; y=−x+3y = -x + 3y=−x+3 at x=−2x = -2x=−2 gives 555 ✔.

The question (for all six parts of Q3): 3. Form the pair of linear equations for the following problems and find their solution by substitution method.

Exercise 3.2, Q3 (i)Two numbers2 marks

Form the pair of linear equations for the following problems and find their solution by substitution method.
(i) The difference between two numbers is 26 and one number is three times the other. Find them.

Given: difference 26; one number is three times the other. Asked: the numbers.

Concept used: the four-step routine with substitution. Why it applies: "three times the other" already gives one number in terms of the other.

  1. 1

    Let the larger number be x and the smaller be y.

  2. 2

    Difference.

    x−y=26(1)x - y = 26 \qquad (1)x−y=26(1)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    One number is three times the other (the larger is 3 times the smaller).

    x=3y(2)x = 3y \qquad (2)x=3y(2)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Substitute (2) into (1).

    3y−y=263y - y = 263y−y=26Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Collect the y-terms.

    2y=262y = 262y=26Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Divide by 2.

    y=13y = 13y=13Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Back-substitute into (2).

    x=39x = 39x=39Swipe to see the whole equation →

  8. Check (story): 39−13=2639 - 13 = 2639−13=26 ✔ and 39=3×1339 = 3 \times 1339=3×13 ✔.

  9. Answer The numbers are 39 and 13.

    Common trap: Writing y=3xy = 3xy=3x while calling x the larger number. Then x−y=−2x=26x - y = -2x = 26x−y=−2x=26 gives x=−13x = -13x=−13, y=−39y = -39y=−39 — and x is not the larger. Decide which is larger before writing the equations. (Negative numbers −13-13−13 and −39-39−39 also differ by 26, with one three times the other; the textbook's answer uses the positive pair.)
Exercise 3.2, Q3 (ii)Supplementary angles2 marks

Form the pair of linear equations for the following problems and find their solution by substitution method.
(ii) The larger of two supplementary angles exceeds the smaller by 18 degrees. Find them.

Given: two supplementary angles (sum 180°); larger − smaller = 18°. Asked: the angles.

Concept used: supplementary angles add up to 180°; substitution. Why it applies: the second fact gives the larger angle in terms of the smaller.

  1. 1

    Let the larger angle be x°x°x° and the smaller be y°y°y°.

  2. 2

    Supplementary.

    x+y=180(1)x + y = 180 \qquad (1)x+y=180(1)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    The larger exceeds the smaller by 18.

    x=y+18(2)x = y + 18 \qquad (2)x=y+18(2)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Substitute (2) into (1).

    (y+18)+y=180(y + 18) + y = 180(y+18)+y=180Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Collect the y-terms.

    2y+18=1802y + 18 = 1802y+18=180Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Subtract 18 from both sides.

    2y=1622y = 1622y=162Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Divide by 2.

    y=81y = 81y=81Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Back-substitute into (2).

    x=99x = 99x=99Swipe to see the whole equation →

  9. Check (story): 99°+81°=180°99° + 81° = 180°99°+81°=180° ✔ and 99°−81°=18°99° - 81° = 18°99°−81°=18° ✔.

  10. Answer The angles are 99° and 81°.

    Common trap: Using 90° (complementary) instead of 180° (supplementary).
Exercise 3.2, Q3 (iii)Bats and balls3 marks

Form the pair of linear equations for the following problems and find their solution by substitution method.
(iii) The coach of a cricket team buys 7 bats and 6 balls for ₹ 3800. Later, she buys 3 bats and 5 balls for ₹ 1750. Find the cost of each bat and each ball.

Given: two purchases. Asked: the cost of one bat and of one ball.

Concept used: the four-step routine with substitution. Why it applies: the question asks for the substitution method.

  1. 1

    Let one bat cost ₹ x and one ball cost ₹ y.

  2. 2

    First purchase.

    7x+6y=3800(1)7x + 6y = 3800 \qquad (1)7x+6y=3800(1)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Second purchase.

    3x+5y=1750(2)3x + 5y = 1750 \qquad (2)3x+5y=1750(2)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    From (2), subtract 5y5y5y from both sides.

    3x=1750−5y3x = 1750 - 5y3x=1750−5ySwipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Divide by 3.

    x=1750−5y3x = \dfrac{1750 - 5y}{3}x=31750−5y​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Substitute into (1).

    7×1750−5y3+6y=38007 \times \dfrac{1750 - 5y}{3} + 6y = 38007×31750−5y​+6y=3800Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Multiply every term by 3.

    7(1750−5y)+18y=114007(1750 - 5y) + 18y = 114007(1750−5y)+18y=11400Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Expand the bracket.

    12250−35y+18y=1140012250 - 35y + 18y = 1140012250−35y+18y=11400Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    Collect the y-terms.

    12250−17y=1140012250 - 17y = 1140012250−17y=11400Swipe to see the whole equation →
  10. 10

    Subtract 12250 from both sides.

    −17y=−850-17y = -850−17y=−850Swipe to see the whole equation →
  11. 11

    Divide by −17-17−17.

    y=50y = 50y=50Swipe to see the whole equation →
  12. 12

    Back-substitute into x=1750−5y3x = \dfrac{1750 - 5y}{3}x=31750−5y​.

    x=1750−2503=15003=500x = \dfrac{1750 - 250}{3} = \dfrac{1500}{3} = 500x=31750−250​=31500​=500Swipe to see the whole equation →

  13. Check (story): 7 bats and 6 balls: 3500+300=38003500 + 300 = 38003500+300=3800 ✔; 3 bats and 5 balls: 1500+250=17501500 + 250 = 17501500+250=1750 ✔.

  14. Answer A bat costs ₹ 500 and a ball costs ₹ 50.

    Common trap: In step 7, multiplying only the fraction by 3 and writing 7(1750−5y)+6y=38007(1750 - 5y) + 6y = 38007(1750−5y)+6y=3800.
Exercise 3.2, Q3 (iv)Taxi charges3 marks

Form the pair of linear equations for the following problems and find their solution by substitution method.
(iv) The taxi charges in a city consist of a fixed charge together with the charge for the distance covered. For a distance of 10 km, the charge paid is ₹ 105 and for a journey of 15 km, the charge paid is ₹ 155. What are the fixed charges and the charge per km? How much does a person have to pay for travelling a distance of 25 km?

Given: two journeys and their charges. Asked: the fixed charge, the charge per km, and the charge for 25 km.

Concept used: total = fixed charge + (charge per km) × distance; substitution. Why it applies: the fixed charge has coefficient 1 in both equations.

  1. 1

    Let the fixed charge be ₹ x and the charge per km be ₹ y.

  2. 2

    10 km journey.

    x+10y=105(1)x + 10y = 105 \qquad (1)x+10y=105(1)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    15 km journey.

    x+15y=155(2)x + 15y = 155 \qquad (2)x+15y=155(2)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    From (1), subtract 10y10y10y from both sides.

    x=105−10yx = 105 - 10yx=105−10ySwipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Substitute into (2).

    105−10y+15y=155105 - 10y + 15y = 155105−10y+15y=155Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Collect the y-terms.

    105+5y=155105 + 5y = 155105+5y=155Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Subtract 105 from both sides.

    5y=505y = 505y=50Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Divide by 5.

    y=10y = 10y=10Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    Back-substitute into x=105−10yx = 105 - 10yx=105−10y.

    x=105−100=5x = 105 - 100 = 5x=105−100=5Swipe to see the whole equation →
  10. 10

    Charge for 25 km.

    x+25y=5+250=255x + 25y = 5 + 250 = 255x+25y=5+250=255Swipe to see the whole equation →

  11. Check (story): 5+10×10=1055 + 10 \times 10 = 1055+10×10=105 ✔; 5+15×10=1555 + 15 \times 10 = 1555+15×10=155 ✔.

  12. Answer Fixed charge ₹ 5, charge ₹ 10 per km; a 25 km journey costs ₹ 255.

    Common trap: Stopping after finding x and y. The last question (25 km) is part of the answer.
Exercise 3.2, Q3 (v)A fraction3 marks

Form the pair of linear equations for the following problems and find their solution by substitution method.
(v) A fraction becomes 911\dfrac{9}{11}119​, if 2 is added to both the numerator and the denominator. If, 3 is added to both the numerator and the denominator it becomes 56\dfrac{5}{6}65​. Find the fraction.

Given: two facts about a fraction. Asked: the fraction.

Concept used: let the fraction be xy\dfrac{x}{y}yx​; cross-multiply each fact; substitution. Why it applies: each fact is an equality of two fractions.

  1. 1

    Let the fraction be xy\dfrac{x}{y}yx​.

  2. 2

    First fact: x+2y+2=911\dfrac{x + 2}{y + 2} = \dfrac{9}{11}y+2x+2​=119​. Cross-multiply.

    11x+22=9y+1811x + 22 = 9y + 1811x+22=9y+18Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Subtract 9y9y9y from both sides.

    11x−9y+22=1811x - 9y + 22 = 1811x−9y+22=18Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Subtract 18 from both sides.

    11x−9y+4=0(1)11x - 9y + 4 = 0 \qquad (1)11x−9y+4=0(1)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Second fact: x+3y+3=56\dfrac{x + 3}{y + 3} = \dfrac{5}{6}y+3x+3​=65​. Cross-multiply.

    6x+18=5y+156x + 18 = 5y + 156x+18=5y+15Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Subtract 5y5y5y from both sides.

    6x−5y+18=156x - 5y + 18 = 156x−5y+18=15Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Subtract 15 from both sides.

    6x−5y+3=0(2)6x - 5y + 3 = 0 \qquad (2)6x−5y+3=0(2)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    From (2), add 5y5y5y to both sides.

    6x+3=5y6x + 3 = 5y6x+3=5ySwipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    Subtract 3 from both sides.

    6x=5y−36x = 5y - 36x=5y−3Swipe to see the whole equation →
  10. 10

    Divide by 6.

    x=5y−36x = \dfrac{5y - 3}{6}x=65y−3​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  11. 11

    Substitute into (1).

    11×5y−36−9y+4=011 \times \dfrac{5y - 3}{6} - 9y + 4 = 011×65y−3​−9y+4=0Swipe to see the whole equation →
  12. 12

    Multiply every term by 6.

    11(5y−3)−54y+24=011(5y - 3) - 54y + 24 = 011(5y−3)−54y+24=0Swipe to see the whole equation →
  13. 13

    Expand the bracket.

    55y−33−54y+24=055y - 33 - 54y + 24 = 055y−33−54y+24=0Swipe to see the whole equation →
  14. 14

    Collect like terms.

    y−9=0y - 9 = 0y−9=0Swipe to see the whole equation →
  15. 15

    Add 9 to both sides.

    y=9y = 9y=9Swipe to see the whole equation →
  16. 16

    Back-substitute into x=5y−36x = \dfrac{5y - 3}{6}x=65y−3​.

    x=45−36=7x = \dfrac{45 - 3}{6} = 7x=645−3​=7Swipe to see the whole equation →

  17. Check (story): 7+29+2=911\dfrac{7 + 2}{9 + 2} = \dfrac{9}{11}9+27+2​=119​ ✔ and 7+39+3=1012=56\dfrac{7 + 3}{9 + 3} = \dfrac{10}{12} = \dfrac{5}{6}9+37+3​=1210​=65​ ✔.

  18. Answer The fraction is 79\dfrac{7}{9}97​.

    Common trap: Cross-multiplying the wrong way round: 9(x+2)=11(y+2)9(x + 2) = 11(y + 2)9(x+2)=11(y+2). The numerator of each side multiplies the denominator of the other side: 11(x+2)=9(y+2)11(x + 2) = 9(y + 2)11(x+2)=9(y+2).
Exercise 3.2, Q3 (vi)Jacob and his son3 marks

Form the pair of linear equations for the following problems and find their solution by substitution method.
(vi) Five years hence, the age of Jacob will be three times that of his son. Five years ago, Jacob's age was seven times that of his son. What are their present ages?

Given: two facts about ages at two times. Asked: present ages.

Concept used: "n years hence/ago" changes both ages by n; substitution. Why it applies: x will have coefficient 1 after rearranging.

  1. 1

    Let Jacob's present age be x years and his son's present age be y years.

  2. 2

    Five years hence both ages are 5 more.

    x+5=3(y+5)x + 5 = 3(y + 5)x+5=3(y+5)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Expand the bracket.

    x+5=3y+15x + 5 = 3y + 15x+5=3y+15Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Subtract 5 from both sides.

    x=3y+10(1)x = 3y + 10 \qquad (1)x=3y+10(1)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Five years ago both ages were 5 less.

    x−5=7(y−5)x - 5 = 7(y - 5)x−5=7(y−5)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Expand the bracket.

    x−5=7y−35x - 5 = 7y - 35x−5=7y−35Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Add 5 to both sides.

    x=7y−30(2)x = 7y - 30 \qquad (2)x=7y−30(2)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Substitute (1) into (2).

    3y+10=7y−303y + 10 = 7y - 303y+10=7y−30Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    Subtract 3y3y3y from both sides.

    10=4y−3010 = 4y - 3010=4y−30Swipe to see the whole equation →
  10. 10

    Add 30 to both sides.

    40=4y40 = 4y40=4ySwipe to see the whole equation →
  11. 11

    Divide by 4.

    y=10y = 10y=10Swipe to see the whole equation →
  12. 12

    Back-substitute into (1).

    x=30+10=40x = 30 + 10 = 40x=30+10=40Swipe to see the whole equation →

  13. Check (story): in 5 years: 45 and 15, and 45=3×1545 = 3 \times 1545=3×15 ✔; 5 years ago: 35 and 5, and 35=7×535 = 7 \times 535=7×5 ✔.

  14. Answer Jacob is 40 years old and his son is 10 years old.

    Common trap: Writing "five years hence" as x+5=3yx + 5 = 3yx+5=3y, adding 5 to Jacob's age only.

Exercise 3.3

The question (for all four parts of Q1): 1. Solve the following pair of linear equations by the elimination method and the substitution method :

Exercise 3.3, Q1 (i)3 marks

Solve the following pair of linear equations by the elimination method and the substitution method :
(i) x+y=5x + y = 5x+y=5 and 2x−3y=42x - 3y = 42x−3y=4

Given: x+y=5x + y = 5x+y=5 and 2x−3y=42x - 3y = 42x−3y=4. Asked: the solution by both methods.

Concept used: elimination (Topic 5) and substitution (Topic 4). Why it applies: the question asks for both; they must agree.

  1. 1

    By elimination

    Multiply every term of x+y=5x + y = 5x+y=5 by 3.

    3x+3y=153x + 3y = 153x+3y=15Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Add 2x−3y=42x - 3y = 42x−3y=4 (the y-coefficients are opposite).

    5x=195x = 195x=19Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Divide by 5.

    x=195x = \dfrac{19}{5}x=519​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Back-substitute into x+y=5x + y = 5x+y=5.

    195+y=5\dfrac{19}{5} + y = 5519​+y=5Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Subtract 195\dfrac{19}{5}519​ from both sides.

    y=65y = \dfrac{6}{5}y=56​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    By substitution

    From x+y=5x + y = 5x+y=5, subtract y from both sides.

    x=5−yx = 5 - yx=5−ySwipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Substitute into 2x−3y=42x - 3y = 42x−3y=4.

    2(5−y)−3y=42(5 - y) - 3y = 42(5−y)−3y=4Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Expand the bracket.

    10−2y−3y=410 - 2y - 3y = 410−2y−3y=4Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    Collect the y-terms.

    10−5y=410 - 5y = 410−5y=4Swipe to see the whole equation →
  10. 10

    Subtract 10 from both sides.

    −5y=−6-5y = -6−5y=−6Swipe to see the whole equation →
  11. 11

    Divide by −5-5−5.

    y=65y = \dfrac{6}{5}y=56​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  12. 12

    Back-substitute into x=5−yx = 5 - yx=5−y.

    x=5−65=195x = 5 - \dfrac{6}{5} = \dfrac{19}{5}x=5−56​=519​Swipe to see the whole equation →

  13. Check: 195+65=255=5\dfrac{19}{5} + \dfrac{6}{5} = \dfrac{25}{5} = 5519​+56​=525​=5 ✔ and 385−185=205=4\dfrac{38}{5} - \dfrac{18}{5} = \dfrac{20}{5} = 4538​−518​=520​=4 ✔. Both methods give the same answer ✔.

  14. Answer x=195x = \dfrac{19}{5}x=519​, y=65y = \dfrac{6}{5}y=56​

    Common trap: Expecting whole numbers and changing a correct fraction. Fractional answers are common; check them in both equations instead.
Exercise 3.3, Q1 (ii)3 marks

Solve the following pair of linear equations by the elimination method and the substitution method :
(ii) 3x+4y=103x + 4y = 103x+4y=10 and 2x−2y=22x - 2y = 22x−2y=2

Given: 3x+4y=103x + 4y = 103x+4y=10 and 2x−2y=22x - 2y = 22x−2y=2. Asked: the solution by both methods.

Concept used: elimination and substitution. Why it applies: both are asked for.

  1. 1

    By elimination

    Multiply every term of 2x−2y=22x - 2y = 22x−2y=2 by 2.

    4x−4y=44x - 4y = 44x−4y=4Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Add 3x+4y=103x + 4y = 103x+4y=10 (the y-coefficients are opposite).

    7x=147x = 147x=14Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Divide by 7.

    x=2x = 2x=2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Back-substitute into 3x+4y=103x + 4y = 103x+4y=10.

    6+4y=106 + 4y = 106+4y=10Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Subtract 6 from both sides.

    4y=44y = 44y=4Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Divide by 4.

    y=1y = 1y=1Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    By substitution

    Divide every term of 2x−2y=22x - 2y = 22x−2y=2 by 2.

    x−y=1x - y = 1x−y=1Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Add y to both sides.

    x=y+1x = y + 1x=y+1Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    Substitute into 3x+4y=103x + 4y = 103x+4y=10.

    3(y+1)+4y=103(y + 1) + 4y = 103(y+1)+4y=10Swipe to see the whole equation →
  10. 10

    Expand the bracket.

    3y+3+4y=103y + 3 + 4y = 103y+3+4y=10Swipe to see the whole equation →
  11. 11

    Collect the y-terms.

    7y+3=107y + 3 = 107y+3=10Swipe to see the whole equation →
  12. 12

    Subtract 3 from both sides.

    7y=77y = 77y=7Swipe to see the whole equation →
  13. 13

    Divide by 7.

    y=1y = 1y=1Swipe to see the whole equation →
  14. 14

    Back-substitute into x=y+1x = y + 1x=y+1.

    x=2x = 2x=2Swipe to see the whole equation →

  15. Check: 3(2)+4(1)=103(2) + 4(1) = 103(2)+4(1)=10 ✔ and 2(2)−2(1)=22(2) - 2(1) = 22(2)−2(1)=2 ✔.

  16. Answer x=2x = 2x=2, y=1y = 1y=1

    Common trap: Multiplying 2x−2y=22x - 2y = 22x−2y=2 by 2 as 4x−4y=24x - 4y = 24x−4y=2 (constant not multiplied), which gives 7x=127x = 127x=12.
Exercise 3.3, Q1 (iii)3 marks

Solve the following pair of linear equations by the elimination method and the substitution method :
(iii) 3x−5y−4=03x - 5y - 4 = 03x−5y−4=0 and 9x=2y+79x = 2y + 79x=2y+7

Given: 3x−5y−4=03x - 5y - 4 = 03x−5y−4=0 and 9x=2y+79x = 2y + 79x=2y+7. Asked: the solution by both methods.

Concept used: line up in the form ax+by=cax + by = cax+by=c, then elimination and substitution. Why it applies: the equations are written in different forms.

  1. 1

    Add 4 to both sides of the first equation.

    3x−5y=43x - 5y = 43x−5y=4Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Subtract 2y2y2y from both sides of the second equation.

    9x−2y=79x - 2y = 79x−2y=7Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    By elimination

    Multiply every term of 3x−5y=43x - 5y = 43x−5y=4 by 3.

    9x−15y=129x - 15y = 129x−15y=12Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Subtract this from 9x−2y=79x - 2y = 79x−2y=7 (the x-coefficients are the same), term by term.

    (9x−9x)+(−2y+15y)=7−12(9x - 9x) + (-2y + 15y) = 7 - 12(9x−9x)+(−2y+15y)=7−12Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Simplify.

    13y=−513y = -513y=−5Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Divide by 13.

    y=−513y = -\dfrac{5}{13}y=−135​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Back-substitute into 3x−5y=43x - 5y = 43x−5y=4.

    3x+2513=43x + \dfrac{25}{13} = 43x+1325​=4Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Subtract 2513\dfrac{25}{13}1325​ from both sides.

    3x=27133x = \dfrac{27}{13}3x=1327​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    Divide by 3.

    x=913x = \dfrac{9}{13}x=139​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  10. 10

    By substitution

    From 3x−5y=43x - 5y = 43x−5y=4, add 5y5y5y to both sides.

    3x=4+5y3x = 4 + 5y3x=4+5ySwipe to see the whole equation →
  11. 11

    Divide by 3.

    x=4+5y3x = \dfrac{4 + 5y}{3}x=34+5y​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  12. 12

    Substitute into 9x−2y=79x - 2y = 79x−2y=7.

    9×4+5y3−2y=79 \times \dfrac{4 + 5y}{3} - 2y = 79×34+5y​−2y=7Swipe to see the whole equation →
  13. 13

    Simplify: 9÷3=39 \div 3 = 39÷3=3.

    3(4+5y)−2y=73(4 + 5y) - 2y = 73(4+5y)−2y=7Swipe to see the whole equation →
  14. 14

    Expand the bracket.

    12+15y−2y=712 + 15y - 2y = 712+15y−2y=7Swipe to see the whole equation →
  15. 15

    Collect the y-terms.

    12+13y=712 + 13y = 712+13y=7Swipe to see the whole equation →
  16. 16

    Subtract 12 from both sides.

    13y=−513y = -513y=−5Swipe to see the whole equation →
  17. 17

    Divide by 13.

    y=−513y = -\dfrac{5}{13}y=−135​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  18. 18

    Back-substitute into x=4+5y3x = \dfrac{4 + 5y}{3}x=34+5y​.

    x=4−25133=2713×13=913x = \dfrac{4 - \dfrac{25}{13}}{3} = \dfrac{27}{13} \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{9}{13}x=34−1325​​=1327​×31​=139​Swipe to see the whole equation →

  19. Check: 3×913−5×(−513)−4=27+25−5213=03 \times \dfrac{9}{13} - 5 \times \left(-\dfrac{5}{13}\right) - 4 = \dfrac{27 + 25 - 52}{13} = 03×139​−5×(−135​)−4=1327+25−52​=0 ✔ and 9×913=81139 \times \dfrac{9}{13} = \dfrac{81}{13}9×139​=1381​, 2×(−513)+7=−10+9113=81132 \times \left(-\dfrac{5}{13}\right) + 7 = \dfrac{-10 + 91}{13} = \dfrac{81}{13}2×(−135​)+7=13−10+91​=1381​ ✔.

  20. Answer x=913x = \dfrac{9}{13}x=139​, y=−513y = -\dfrac{5}{13}y=−135​

    Common trap: Writing 9x=2y+79x = 2y + 79x=2y+7 as 9x+2y=79x + 2y = 79x+2y=7 when lining up. The 2y2y2y changes sign when it moves.
Exercise 3.3, Q1 (iv)3 marks

Solve the following pair of linear equations by the elimination method and the substitution method :
(iv) x2+2y3=−1\dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{2y}{3} = -12x​+32y​=−1 and x−y3=3x - \dfrac{y}{3} = 3x−3y​=3

Given: two equations with fractions. Asked: the solution by both methods.

Concept used: clear fractions, then elimination and substitution. Why it applies: whole-number coefficients first.

  1. 1

    Multiply every term of the first equation by 6.

    3x+4y=−63x + 4y = -63x+4y=−6Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Multiply every term of the second equation by 3.

    3x−y=93x - y = 93x−y=9Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    By elimination

    Subtract the second from the first (the x-coefficients are the same), term by term.

    (3x−3x)+(4y−(−y))=−6−9(3x - 3x) + (4y - (-y)) = -6 - 9(3x−3x)+(4y−(−y))=−6−9Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Simplify.

    5y=−155y = -155y=−15Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Divide by 5.

    y=−3y = -3y=−3Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Back-substitute into 3x−y=93x - y = 93x−y=9.

    3x+3=93x + 3 = 93x+3=9Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Subtract 3 from both sides.

    3x=63x = 63x=6Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Divide by 3.

    x=2x = 2x=2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    By substitution

    From 3x−y=93x - y = 93x−y=9, add y to both sides.

    3x=9+y3x = 9 + y3x=9+ySwipe to see the whole equation →
  10. 10

    Subtract 9 from both sides.

    y=3x−9y = 3x - 9y=3x−9Swipe to see the whole equation →
  11. 11

    Substitute into 3x+4y=−63x + 4y = -63x+4y=−6.

    3x+4(3x−9)=−63x + 4(3x - 9) = -63x+4(3x−9)=−6Swipe to see the whole equation →
  12. 12

    Expand the bracket.

    3x+12x−36=−63x + 12x - 36 = -63x+12x−36=−6Swipe to see the whole equation →
  13. 13

    Collect the x-terms.

    15x−36=−615x - 36 = -615x−36=−6Swipe to see the whole equation →
  14. 14

    Add 36 to both sides.

    15x=3015x = 3015x=30Swipe to see the whole equation →
  15. 15

    Divide by 15.

    x=2x = 2x=2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  16. 16

    Back-substitute into y=3x−9y = 3x - 9y=3x−9.

    y=6−9=−3y = 6 - 9 = -3y=6−9=−3Swipe to see the whole equation →

  17. Check: 22+2(−3)3=1−2=−1\dfrac{2}{2} + \dfrac{2(-3)}{3} = 1 - 2 = -122​+32(−3)​=1−2=−1 ✔ and 2−−33=2+1=32 - \dfrac{-3}{3} = 2 + 1 = 32−3−3​=2+1=3 ✔.

  18. Answer x=2x = 2x=2, y=−3y = -3y=−3

    Common trap: In step 3, writing 4y−(−y)=3y4y - (-y) = 3y4y−(−y)=3y. Subtracting −y-y−y adds y: 4y+y=5y4y + y = 5y4y+y=5y.

The question (for all five parts of Q2): 2. Form the pair of linear equations in the following problems, and find their solutions (if they exist) by the elimination method :

Exercise 3.3, Q2 (i)A fraction3 marks

Form the pair of linear equations in the following problems, and find their solutions (if they exist) by the elimination method :
(i) If we add 1 to the numerator and subtract 1 from the denominator, a fraction reduces to 1. It becomes 12\dfrac{1}{2}21​ if we only add 1 to the denominator. What is the fraction?

Given: two facts about a fraction. Asked: the fraction.

Concept used: let the fraction be xy\dfrac{x}{y}yx​; elimination. Why it applies: both equations will have −y-y−y.

  1. 1

    Let the fraction be xy\dfrac{x}{y}yx​.

  2. 2

    First fact.

    x+1y−1=1\dfrac{x + 1}{y - 1} = 1y−1x+1​=1Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Multiply both sides by (y−1)(y - 1)(y−1).

    x+1=y−1x + 1 = y - 1x+1=y−1Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Subtract y from both sides.

    x−y+1=−1x - y + 1 = -1x−y+1=−1Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Subtract 1 from both sides.

    x−y=−2(1)x - y = -2 \qquad (1)x−y=−2(1)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Second fact (only the denominator changes).

    xy+1=12\dfrac{x}{y + 1} = \dfrac{1}{2}y+1x​=21​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Cross-multiply.

    2x=y+12x = y + 12x=y+1Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Subtract y from both sides.

    2x−y=1(2)2x - y = 1 \qquad (2)2x−y=1(2)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    Subtract (1) from (2), term by term.

    (2x−x)+(−y+y)=1−(−2)(2x - x) + (-y + y) = 1 - (-2)(2x−x)+(−y+y)=1−(−2)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  10. 10

    Simplify.

    x=3x = 3x=3Swipe to see the whole equation →
  11. 11

    Back-substitute into (1).

    3−y=−23 - y = -23−y=−2Swipe to see the whole equation →
  12. 12

    Subtract 3 from both sides.

    −y=−5-y = -5−y=−5Swipe to see the whole equation →
  13. 13

    Multiply both sides by −1-1−1.

    y=5y = 5y=5Swipe to see the whole equation →

  14. Check (story): 3+15−1=44=1\dfrac{3 + 1}{5 - 1} = \dfrac{4}{4} = 15−13+1​=44​=1 ✔ and 35+1=36=12\dfrac{3}{5 + 1} = \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}5+13​=63​=21​ ✔.

  15. Answer The fraction is 35\dfrac{3}{5}53​.

    Common trap: Writing the second fact as x+1y+1=12\dfrac{x + 1}{y + 1} = \dfrac{1}{2}y+1x+1​=21​. The word "only" means the numerator is unchanged.
Exercise 3.3, Q2 (ii)Nuri and Sonu3 marks

Form the pair of linear equations in the following problems, and find their solutions (if they exist) by the elimination method :
(ii) Five years ago, Nuri was thrice as old as Sonu. Ten years later, Nuri will be twice as old as Sonu. How old are Nuri and Sonu?

Given: two facts about ages. Asked: present ages.

Concept used: "n years ago/later" changes both ages by n; elimination. Why it applies: both equations will have x with coefficient 1.

  1. 1

    Let Nuri's present age be x years and Sonu's be y years.

  2. 2

    Five years ago both were 5 years younger.

    x−5=3(y−5)x - 5 = 3(y - 5)x−5=3(y−5)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Expand the bracket.

    x−5=3y−15x - 5 = 3y - 15x−5=3y−15Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Subtract 3y3y3y from both sides.

    x−3y−5=−15x - 3y - 5 = -15x−3y−5=−15Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Add 5 to both sides.

    x−3y=−10(1)x - 3y = -10 \qquad (1)x−3y=−10(1)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Ten years later both will be 10 years older.

    x+10=2(y+10)x + 10 = 2(y + 10)x+10=2(y+10)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Expand the bracket.

    x+10=2y+20x + 10 = 2y + 20x+10=2y+20Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Subtract 2y2y2y from both sides.

    x−2y+10=20x - 2y + 10 = 20x−2y+10=20Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    Subtract 10 from both sides.

    x−2y=10(2)x - 2y = 10 \qquad (2)x−2y=10(2)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  10. 10

    Subtract (1) from (2), term by term.

    (x−x)+(−2y+3y)=10−(−10)(x - x) + (-2y + 3y) = 10 - (-10)(x−x)+(−2y+3y)=10−(−10)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  11. 11

    Simplify.

    y=20y = 20y=20Swipe to see the whole equation →
  12. 12

    Back-substitute into (2).

    x−40=10x - 40 = 10x−40=10Swipe to see the whole equation →
  13. 13

    Add 40 to both sides.

    x=50x = 50x=50Swipe to see the whole equation →

  14. Check (story): five years ago: 45 and 15, 45=3×1545 = 3 \times 1545=3×15 ✔; ten years later: 60 and 30, 60=2×3060 = 2 \times 3060=2×30 ✔.

  15. Answer Nuri is 50 years old and Sonu is 20 years old.

    Common trap: 10−(−10)10 - (-10)10−(−10) computed as 0. Subtracting a negative adds: 10+10=2010 + 10 = 2010+10=20.
Exercise 3.3, Q2 (iii)A two-digit number3 marks

Form the pair of linear equations in the following problems, and find their solutions (if they exist) by the elimination method :
(iii) The sum of the digits of a two-digit number is 9. Also, nine times this number is twice the number obtained by reversing the order of the digits. Find the number.

Given: digit sum 9; 9 × number = 2 × reversed number. Asked: the number.

Concept used: number =10x+y= 10x + y=10x+y, reversed =10y+x= 10y + x=10y+x; elimination. Why it applies: the second fact compares the number with its reverse.

  1. 1

    Let the tens digit be x and the units digit be y. The number is 10x+y10x + y10x+y; reversed, 10y+x10y + x10y+x.

  2. 2

    Sum of the digits.

    x+y=9(1)x + y = 9 \qquad (1)x+y=9(1)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Nine times the number is twice the reversed number.

    9(10x+y)=2(10y+x)9(10x + y) = 2(10y + x)9(10x+y)=2(10y+x)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Expand both sides.

    90x+9y=20y+2x90x + 9y = 20y + 2x90x+9y=20y+2xSwipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Subtract 2x2x2x from both sides.

    88x+9y=20y88x + 9y = 20y88x+9y=20ySwipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Subtract 20y20y20y from both sides.

    88x−11y=088x - 11y = 088x−11y=0Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Divide by 11.

    8x−y=0(2)8x - y = 0 \qquad (2)8x−y=0(2)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Add (1) and (2) (the y-coefficients are opposite).

    9x=99x = 99x=9Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    Divide by 9.

    x=1x = 1x=1Swipe to see the whole equation →
  10. 10

    Back-substitute into (1).

    1+y=91 + y = 91+y=9Swipe to see the whole equation →
  11. 11

    Subtract 1 from both sides.

    y=8y = 8y=8Swipe to see the whole equation →

  12. Check (story): the number is 18; 1+8=91 + 8 = 91+8=9 ✔; 9×18=1629 \times 18 = 1629×18=162 and 2×81=1622 \times 81 = 1622×81=162 ✔.

  13. Answer The number is 18.

    Common trap: Writing the number as x+yx + yx+y (the digit sum) in the second equation.
Exercise 3.3, Q2 (iv)Notes from the bank3 marks

Form the pair of linear equations in the following problems, and find their solutions (if they exist) by the elimination method :
(iv) Meena went to a bank to withdraw ₹ 2000. She asked the cashier to give her ₹ 50 and ₹ 100 notes only. Meena got 25 notes in all. Find how many notes of ₹ 50 and ₹ 100 she received.

Given: 25 notes; total value ₹ 2000. Asked: the number of each note.

Concept used: the number of notes and the value of the notes; elimination. Why it applies: after dividing the value equation by 50, both equations have x with coefficient 1.

  1. 1

    Let the number of ₹ 50 notes be x and the number of ₹ 100 notes be y.

  2. 2

    Number of notes.

    x+y=25(1)x + y = 25 \qquad (1)x+y=25(1)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Value of the notes.

    50x+100y=200050x + 100y = 200050x+100y=2000Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Divide every term by 50.

    x+2y=40(2)x + 2y = 40 \qquad (2)x+2y=40(2)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Subtract (1) from (2), term by term.

    (x−x)+(2y−y)=40−25(x - x) + (2y - y) = 40 - 25(x−x)+(2y−y)=40−25Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Simplify.

    y=15y = 15y=15Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Back-substitute into (1).

    x+15=25x + 15 = 25x+15=25Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Subtract 15 from both sides.

    x=10x = 10x=10Swipe to see the whole equation →

  9. Check (story): 10+15=2510 + 15 = 2510+15=25 notes ✔; 10×50+15×100=500+1500=200010 \times 50 + 15 \times 100 = 500 + 1500 = 200010×50+15×100=500+1500=2000 ✔.

  10. Answer 10 notes of ₹ 50 and 15 notes of ₹ 100.

    Common trap: Writing x+y=2000x + y = 2000x+y=2000 — mixing the number of notes with their value.
Exercise 3.3, Q2 (v)A lending library3 marks

Form the pair of linear equations in the following problems, and find their solutions (if they exist) by the elimination method :
(v) A lending library has a fixed charge for the first three days and an additional charge for each day thereafter. Saritha paid ₹ 27 for a book kept for seven days, while Susy paid ₹ 21 for the book she kept for five days. Find the fixed charge and the charge for each extra day.

Given: the fixed charge covers the first 3 days; two bills. Asked: the fixed charge and the charge per extra day.

Concept used: total = fixed charge + (extra days) × (charge per day); elimination. Why it applies: the fixed charge appears in both bills.

  1. 1

    Let the fixed charge be ₹ x and the charge for each extra day be ₹ y.

  2. 2

    Saritha: 7 days = 3 days + 4 extra days.

    x+4y=27(1)x + 4y = 27 \qquad (1)x+4y=27(1)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Susy: 5 days = 3 days + 2 extra days.

    x+2y=21(2)x + 2y = 21 \qquad (2)x+2y=21(2)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Subtract (2) from (1), term by term.

    (x−x)+(4y−2y)=27−21(x - x) + (4y - 2y) = 27 - 21(x−x)+(4y−2y)=27−21Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Simplify.

    2y=62y = 62y=6Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Divide by 2.

    y=3y = 3y=3Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Back-substitute into (2).

    x+6=21x + 6 = 21x+6=21Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Subtract 6 from both sides.

    x=15x = 15x=15Swipe to see the whole equation →

  9. Check (story): Saritha: 15+4×3=2715 + 4 \times 3 = 2715+4×3=27 ✔; Susy: 15+2×3=2115 + 2 \times 3 = 2115+2×3=21 ✔.

  10. Answer Fixed charge ₹ 15; ₹ 3 for each extra day.

    Common trap: Using 7 and 5 days instead of the extra days: x+7y=27x + 7y = 27x+7y=27 and x+5y=21x + 5y = 21x+5y=21 give y=3y = 3y=3 but x=6x = 6x=6 — a fixed charge that does not fit the story.
